subject: Physiology
summary: The RAAS links kidney perfusion to systemic blood pressure and fluid balance. It adjusts vascular tone, sodium reabsorption, and aldosterone release to maintain circulatory homeostasis.

sections.p: When renal perfusion falls, the kidneys launch a hormonal cascade that raises blood pressure and conserves salt and water.
b: Key organs: juxtaglomerular cells, liver, lungs, adrenal cortex
Main hormones: renin, angiotensin I & II, aldosterone

sections.p: Low stretch of the afferent arteriole → juxtaglomerular cells release renin → renin cleaves hepatic angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → ACE in lung endothelium converts to angiotensin II → angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal zona glomerulosa.
b: Angiotensin II raises systemic vascular resistance
Aldosterone increases Na⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct

t.b: Is renin over‑ or under‑produced? High renin suggests volume depletion or renal artery stenosis; low renin points to primary hyperaldosteronism.
Is aldosterone excess present? Elevated aldosterone with low renin indicates primary hyperaldosteronism; both high suggests secondary causes.

sections.p: Negative feedback from blood pressure, sodium load, and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) dampens renin release; sympathetic nerves and β‑1 stimulation increase it.
b: Low BP → increased sympathetic tone → ↑ renin

sections.p: Both excess and deficiency of RAAS cause disease. Over‑activation leads to hypertension, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease; under‑activation causes hypotension and salt‑wasting.
b: Primary hyperaldosteronism: adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia → resistant hypertension, hypokalemia
Renovascular hypertension: renal artery stenosis → high renin, secondary hypertension

t.b: Is there stenosis? Detects >70% narrowing; if unavailable, use CT angiography or captopril renography.
Is hypokalemia present? Low K⁺ supports aldosterone excess; normal K⁺ does not rule it out.

sections.p: RAAS manipulation is central to treating hypertension, heart failure, and proteinuric kidney disease. Understanding its physiology guides drug choice and monitoring.
b: ACE inhibitors block conversion of Ang I → Ang II, lowering BP and reducing proteinuria
ARBs block Ang II receptors, useful when ACE inhibitors cause cough
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists block aldosterone effects, sparing K⁺

sections.p: Focus on the cascade steps, feedback loops, and how each drug class intervenes.
b: Renin ↑ → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II → AT1 receptor → vasoconstriction + aldosterone
Primary hyperaldosteronism: high aldosterone, low renin, hypertension, hypokalemia
ACE‑I contraindicated in pregnancy; monitor creatinine and K⁺ after start

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 with end‑organ damage)
Sudden onset of refractory hypokalemia causing arrhythmia
Acute renal artery occlusion presenting with flank pain and anuria

faq.q: Why does ACE inhibition lower proteinuria?
faq.a: Angiotensin II constricts efferent arterioles, raising glomerular pressure; ACE‑I dilates them, reducing pressure and protein leak.
Yes, primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin while aldosterone drives sodium retention and high BP.

faq.q: What is the role of ANP in RAAS?
faq.a: ANP released from atria inhibits renin release and opposes aldosterone, promoting natriuresis.

exam: Explain how renal artery stenosis leads to secondary hypertension and which lab values you would expect.
Describe the mechanism by which ACE inhibitors improve outcomes in diabetic nephropathy.
List the clinical clues that differentiate primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism.
